title: Describing Change
subtitle: Compare then and now, describe trends, and tell the story of how your life changed

lessons.title: Avant / maintenant
lessons.description: Use the imparfait and the présent side by side to describe how things used to be and how they are now.

blocks.heading: Then and now: imparfait vs présent
blocks.body: When you compare how life used to be with how it is today, French leans on two tenses: the imparfait for the old picture and the présent for the current one. The imparfait describes a state or habit that was ongoing, with no clear end in mind — perfect for setting a scene from the past.

examples.french: Avant, je vivais à la campagne.
examples.english: Before, I used to live in the countryside.

examples.french: Maintenant, j'habite en ville.
examples.english: Now, I live in the city.

examples.french: On mangeait plus lentement, autrefois.
examples.english: People used to eat more slowly, in the old days.

examples.french: Aujourd'hui, tout va plus vite.
examples.english: Today, everything moves faster.

examples.french: Elle ne travaillait pas ; maintenant, elle est cheffe d'entreprise.
examples.english: She didn't use to work; now, she's a company head.

blocks.tip: Think of the imparfait as a paused photo of the past and the présent as a live video of today — the contrast is the whole point of this lesson.

blocks.heading: Time markers for contrast
blocks.body: A handful of adverbs and expressions do the heavy lifting when you contrast past and present: "avant", "autrefois" and "à l'époque" point backwards, while "maintenant", "aujourd'hui", "de nos jours", "désormais" and "actuellement" point to today. Placing one of each in the same sentence makes the change obvious.

examples.french: Autrefois, on écrivait des lettres ; de nos jours, on envoie des messages.
examples.english: In the old days, people wrote letters; nowadays, people send messages.

examples.french: À l'époque, personne n'avait de portable.
examples.english: Back then, nobody had a mobile phone.

examples.french: Désormais, tout le monde est connecté en permanence.
examples.english: From now on, everyone is permanently connected.

examples.french: Actuellement, je travaille à mi-temps.
examples.english: Currently, I work part-time.

blocks.tip: "Actuellement" means "currently", not "actually" — a classic false friend to watch for.

blocks.heading: Talking about what's no longer true
blocks.body: To say something has stopped being the case, use "ne ... plus" (no longer). To say it's still true, use "encore" or "toujours" — but note "toujours" is ambiguous: it can mean "always" or "still", depending on context.

examples.french: Je ne fume plus depuis deux ans.
examples.english: I no longer smoke, for two years now.

examples.french: Il n'habite plus chez ses parents.
examples.english: He no longer lives with his parents.

examples.french: Elle travaille encore le samedi.
examples.english: She still works on Saturdays.

examples.french: Il est toujours aussi curieux.
examples.english: He's still just as curious.

blocks.tip: Context tells you which "toujours" you're hearing: with a state that could change, it usually means "still".

blocks.heading: Forming and using the imparfait
blocks.body: Take the "nous" form of the présent, drop "-ons", and add: -ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient. Only "être" is irregular in its stem (ét-). Use the imparfait for descriptions, habits, and background states in the past — exactly what you need to paint the "before" picture.

examples.french: Nous habitions un petit village.
examples.english: We used to live in a small village.

examples.french: J'étais plus timide, avant.
examples.english: I used to be shyer, before.

examples.french: Tu prenais toujours le même chemin.
examples.english: You always used to take the same path.

examples.french: Ils travaillaient six jours sur sept.
examples.english: They used to work six days out of seven.

blocks.tip: The imparfait describes; the passé composé narrates a single completed event. "Avant/maintenant" contrasts almost always use the imparfait for the past side.

blocks.heading: Building a then/now sentence
blocks.body: A strong then/now sentence usually has three parts: a time marker for the past (avant, autrefois), the imparfait, and a contrasting time marker for the present (maintenant, aujourd'hui) with the présent. Link the two halves with "mais", "alors que" or simply a semicolon.

examples.french: Avant, on écrivait des lettres ; maintenant, on envoie des emails.
examples.english: Before, people wrote letters; now, they send emails.

examples.french: Autrefois, elle vivait seule, alors qu'aujourd'hui elle a une grande famille.
examples.english: In the past, she lived alone, whereas today she has a big family.

examples.french: À l'époque, je ne cuisinais jamais ; désormais, je cuisine tous les soirs.
examples.english: Back then, I never cooked; now, I cook every evening.

blocks.tip: "Alors que" is a very useful B1 connector for contrast — it works for both time and opposition, so it fits perfectly in this lesson.

passages.title: Mon quartier, avant et maintenant
passages.french:
Quand j'étais enfant, mon quartier était très différent d'aujourd'hui.
Il y avait un grand marché tous les samedis, avec des odeurs de pain chaud et de fruits frais.
Les voisins se connaissaient tous et on laissait souvent la porte ouverte.
Autrefois, il n'y avait presque pas de voitures dans notre petite rue.
On jouait dehors jusqu'au soir, sans avoir peur de rien.
Aujourd'hui, tout a changé.
Le marché a disparu ; à sa place, il y a un grand supermarché moderne.
De nos jours, les gens se parlent moins, même s'ils habitent porte à porte.
Il y a beaucoup plus de circulation, et les enfants jouent surtout à l'intérieur.
Je me rends compte que ce n'est plus vraiment le même endroit.
Pourtant, par rapport à avant, le quartier est plus propre et mieux éclairé.
Je ne sais pas si c'est un vrai progrès, ou juste un changement de plus.
passages.english:
When I was a child, my neighbourhood was very different from today.
There was a big market every Saturday, with smells of warm bread and fresh fruit.
The neighbours all knew each other and we often left the door open.
In the old days, there were almost no cars in our little street.
We played outside until evening, without being afraid of anything.
Today, everything has changed.
The market has disappeared; in its place, there's a big modern supermarket.
Nowadays, people talk to each other less, even if they live door to door.
There's much more traffic, and children mostly play indoors.
I realize that it's not really the same place anymore.
And yet, compared with before, the neighbourhood is cleaner and better lit.
I don't know if it's real progress, or just one more change.

lessons.title: Les tendances
lessons.description: Describe rising and falling trends, talk about statistics, and say what's becoming more or less popular.

blocks.heading: Reading a trend
blocks.body: French uses a small set of verbs and nouns to describe a line going up or down: "augmenter"/"la hausse" for a rise, "diminuer"/"la baisse" for a fall, and "la tendance" for the general direction. These words appear constantly in the news, in graphs, and in everyday conversation about prices, habits, or opinions.

examples.french: Le nombre d'utilisateurs augmente chaque année.
examples.english: The number of users increases every year.

examples.french: On observe une nette baisse des ventes.
examples.english: We're seeing a marked drop in sales.

examples.french: La tendance est clairement à la hausse.
examples.english: The trend is clearly upward.

examples.french: Ce chiffre a doublé en cinq ans.
examples.english: This figure has doubled in five years.

examples.french: Le taux de participation a diminué depuis 2010.
examples.english: The turnout rate has decreased since 2010.

blocks.tip: "La hausse" and "la baisse" are nouns — use them after "en" (en hausse, en baisse) or "à la" (à la hausse).

blocks.heading: Talking in percentages and fractions
blocks.body: Statistics rarely stop at whole numbers. You'll need "le pourcentage", "la moyenne" (the average), and fraction words like "la moitié" (half), "le tiers" (a third), "la majorité" and "la minorité". "Environ" softens a figure when it's approximate.

examples.french: Vingt pour cent des Français ont changé de métier.
examples.english: Twenty percent of French people have changed careers.

examples.french: La moitié des sondés disent avoir changé d'avis.
examples.english: Half of those surveyed say they've changed their minds.

examples.french: Un tiers de la population vit désormais en ville.
examples.english: A third of the population now lives in cities.

examples.french: En moyenne, ce chiffre a augmenté de dix points.
examples.english: On average, this figure has increased by ten points.

blocks.tip: "La majorité" takes a singular verb in French even when it clearly refers to many people: "la majorité pense que...".

blocks.heading: What's popular and what's not
blocks.body: To describe a growing or shrinking trend in popularity, use "de plus en plus" (more and more) or "de moins en moins" (less and less) before an adjective or a verb. Combine them with "populaire" and "la popularité" to talk about fashions, habits, and opinions.

examples.french: Ce sport devient de plus en plus populaire.
examples.english: This sport is becoming more and more popular.

examples.french: Les gens lisent de moins en moins la presse papier.
examples.english: People read the print press less and less.

examples.french: Sa popularité a beaucoup grandi cette année.
examples.english: His popularity has grown a lot this year.

examples.french: Selon un sondage récent, cette idée séduit de plus en plus.
examples.english: According to a recent poll, this idea is winning more and more people over.

blocks.tip: "De plus en plus" and "de moins en moins" never change form — no agreement needed, which makes them easy to reuse.

blocks.heading: Expressing proportions
blocks.body: To say what share of a group does something, use "la moitié de", "le tiers de", "la majorité de" or a percentage, followed by "de" + a plural noun, and a plural verb. "Un/une ... sur ..." (one in ...) is another very natural way to express a proportion.

examples.french: La moitié des Français ont déjà changé de métier.
examples.english: Half of French people have already changed jobs.

examples.french: Un Français sur trois dit avoir changé d'avis.
examples.english: One French person in three says they've changed their mind.

examples.french: La majorité des sondés approuvent cette évolution.
examples.english: The majority of those surveyed approve of this change.

blocks.tip: Even though "la moitié", "le tiers" and "la majorité" are singular nouns, the verb that follows "de + plural noun" is usually plural, agreeing with the people counted.

blocks.heading: Describing movement with passer de ... à
blocks.body: "Passer de ... à ..." is the standard way to describe a figure moving from one value to another over time. Combine it with "en + [number of years]" to show how fast the change happened.

examples.french: Le taux est passé de 10 % à 25 % en cinq ans.
examples.english: The rate went from 10% to 25% in five years.

examples.french: Le nombre d'utilisateurs est passé de cent à mille.
examples.english: The number of users went from a hundred to a thousand.

examples.french: Ce chiffre est passé de la baisse à la hausse.
examples.english: This figure went from falling to rising.

blocks.tip: "Passer de X à Y" always uses "être" as the auxiliary in the passé composé: "il est passé de ... à ...".

passages.title: Le télétravail : ce que dit le sondage
passages.french:
Un nouveau sondage vient de paraître sur les habitudes de travail des Français.
Selon cette étude, le télétravail est de plus en plus populaire depuis quelques années.
En effet, le pourcentage de salariés qui travaillent au moins un jour par semaine à la maison a doublé depuis 2019.
La moitié des personnes interrogées disent préférer ce nouveau rythme de vie.
Cependant, un tiers d'entre elles constatent aussi un sentiment d'isolement.
Le graphique publié avec le sondage montre une courbe qui monte régulièrement.
La tendance touche surtout les grandes villes, où le taux dépasse la moyenne nationale.
À la campagne, en revanche, le chiffre reste plus stable.
D'après les chercheurs, cette évolution est loin d'être terminée.
Ils prévoient que ce taux continuera d'augmenter dans les prochaines années.
La minorité qui reste opposée au télétravail invoque surtout la difficulté à se concentrer.
Une chose est sûre : nos habitudes de travail ne ressemblent plus à celles d'avant.
passages.english:
A new poll has just been published on the working habits of French people.
According to this study, remote work has become more and more popular in recent years.
Indeed, the percentage of employees who work from home at least one day a week has doubled since 2019.
Half of the people surveyed say they prefer this new pace of life.
However, a third of them also note a feeling of isolation.
The chart published with the poll shows a steadily rising line.
The trend mostly affects big cities, where the rate exceeds the national average.
In the countryside, on the other hand, the figure remains more stable.
According to the researchers, this change is far from over.
They predict that this rate will keep increasing in the coming years.
The minority who remain opposed to remote work mostly cite difficulty concentrating.
One thing is certain: our working habits no longer resemble what they used to be.

lessons.title: Ma vie a changé
lessons.description: Tell the story of a personal change, from the turning point to how you feel about it today.

blocks.heading: The turning point
blocks.body: Every personal change story has a moment where things shifted — a "tournant" (turning point) or a "déclic" (the click, the moment it suddenly made sense). French marks this moment with the passé composé, since it's a single completed event, even if the story around it uses the imparfait.

examples.french: Il y a eu un vrai tournant dans ma vie l'année dernière.
examples.english: There was a real turning point in my life last year.

examples.french: J'ai eu un déclic le jour de mon trentième anniversaire.
examples.english: I had a moment of realization on my thirtieth birthday.

examples.french: J'ai décidé de tout changer.
examples.english: I decided to change everything.

examples.french: J'ai enfin osé partir.
examples.english: I finally dared to leave.

blocks.tip: "Le déclic" is a very B1-idiomatic way to say "the moment it clicked" — French speakers use it constantly in personal stories.

blocks.heading: The process of change
blocks.body: After the turning point comes the process: getting used to a new life, adapting, growing. "S'adapter", "s'habituer à" and "grandir" describe this gradual movement, often in the imparfait if you're describing what the process felt like, or the passé composé if you're marking its completion.

examples.french: Je me suis adapté petit à petit à ma nouvelle vie.
examples.english: I gradually adapted to my new life.

examples.french: Il a fallu du temps pour m'habituer à ce rythme.
examples.english: It took time to get used to this pace.

examples.french: J'ai beaucoup grandi pendant cette période.
examples.english: I grew a lot during that period.

examples.french: Je progressais chaque semaine, sans m'en rendre compte.
examples.english: I was progressing every week, without realizing it.

blocks.tip: "Petit à petit" (little by little) pairs naturally with change verbs to show the process wasn't instant.

blocks.heading: Looking back
blocks.body: To close a change story, French speakers often step back and reflect using "avec le recul" (looking back, in hindsight), and describe how they feel now with words like "la fierté" (pride) and "la confiance en soi" (self-confidence).

examples.french: Avec le recul, je ne regrette rien.
examples.english: Looking back, I regret nothing.

examples.french: Je suis fier du chemin parcouru.
examples.english: I'm proud of how far I've come.

examples.french: J'ai gagné en confiance en moi.
examples.english: I've gained self-confidence.

examples.french: Depuis ce changement, je me sens enfin épanoui.
examples.english: Since that change, I finally feel fulfilled.

blocks.tip: "Le chemin parcouru" (literally "the path travelled") is a lovely fixed image for describing personal progress.

blocks.heading: Passé composé vs imparfait in a change narrative
blocks.body: A personal change story usually mixes both past tenses: the imparfait sets the scene ("before, I was...") and the passé composé marks the single event that changed everything ("then, I decided..."). Getting this contrast right is what makes a story sound natural rather than like a list of facts.

examples.french: Avant, j'étais plutôt timide, mais un jour, j'ai osé changer de vie.
examples.english: Before, I was rather shy, but one day, I dared to change my life.

examples.french: Je travaillais dans la finance quand j'ai décidé de tout quitter.
examples.english: I was working in finance when I decided to leave everything.

examples.french: Je ne savais pas ce que je voulais, jusqu'au jour où j'ai eu un déclic.
examples.english: I didn't know what I wanted, until the day I had a realization.

blocks.tip: A useful pattern: imparfait + "quand" + passé composé — it captures the background interrupted by the turning-point event.

blocks.heading: Depuis que + présent, and avant de + infinitive
blocks.body: "Depuis que" (ever since) is followed by a clause, usually in the présent if the effect is ongoing. "Avant de" + infinitive and "après avoir/être" + past participle are useful for sequencing the steps of your story without repeating the subject.

examples.french: Depuis que j'ai déménagé, je me sens plus libre.
examples.english: Ever since I moved, I've felt freer.

examples.french: Avant de partir, j'ai longuement réfléchi.
examples.english: Before leaving, I thought about it for a long time.

examples.french: Après avoir surmonté mes peurs, j'ai enfin osé me lancer.
examples.english: After overcoming my fears, I finally dared to take the plunge.

blocks.tip: "Avant de" and "après avoir/être" both require the same subject in both halves of the sentence — otherwise, use "avant que" + subjunctive.

passages.title: Ma vie a changé
passages.french:
Il y a cinq ans, je travaillais dans un bureau, du lundi au vendredi, sans jamais me poser de questions.
J'étais plutôt content de ma vie, ou du moins je le croyais.
Puis, un jour, j'ai eu un vrai déclic.
Je me suis rendu compte que je n'étais pas épanoui dans ce métier.
Après avoir longuement réfléchi, j'ai décidé de tout quitter pour me lancer dans la pâtisserie.
Ma famille pensait que c'était une erreur, mais j'ai osé le faire quand même.
Les premiers mois ont été difficiles : j'ai dû recommencer à zéro et apprendre un nouveau métier.
Petit à petit, je me suis adapté à ce nouveau rythme de vie.
J'ai surmonté beaucoup d'obstacles, et j'ai gagné en confiance en moi.
Aujourd'hui, je tiens ma propre boulangerie, et je me sens enfin à ma place.
Avec le recul, ce tournant a été la meilleure décision de ma vie.
Je suis fier du chemin parcouru depuis ce jour-là.
passages.english:
Five years ago, I worked in an office, Monday to Friday, never asking myself any questions.
I was fairly happy with my life, or at least I thought so.
Then, one day, I had a real moment of realization.
I realized I wasn't fulfilled in that job.
After thinking it over for a long time, I decided to leave everything to go into pastry-making.
My family thought it was a mistake, but I dared to do it anyway.
The first months were hard: I had to start from scratch and learn a new trade.
Little by little, I adapted to this new pace of life.
I overcame many obstacles, and I gained self-confidence.
Today, I run my own bakery, and I finally feel like I'm where I belong.
Looking back, that turning point was the best decision of my life.
I'm proud of how far I've come since that day.
